newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Looming power crisis worries Sri Lanka business.
newsitem.headline: Looming power crisis worries Sri Lanka business.

text.p: The possibility of power cuts has Sri Lankan business worried despite government assurances that last year's drought-related blackouts will not be repeated, industry officials said on Tuesday.
"The government has given us an assurance there will be no power cuts," said Patrick Amerasinghe, president of the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
"In spite of all that, we are concerend there might be even a partial repetiton of last year," he told Reuters.
"Our members are getting concerned and they have begun to watch the situation closely," said Ashroff Omar, chairman of the Apparel Exporters Association.
"But instead of waiting for rain, we are encouraging our members to generate their own power, making use of the concessions government has given," he said.

Tropical Sri Lanka, which relies on hydropower for nearly 85 percent of its electricity supply, is experiencing a drought for the second consecutive year, lowering water levels in reservoirs to dangerous levels and threatening power cuts.

Last year, the failure of the November-March northeast monsoon and the delayed onset of the mid-year southwest monsoon, forced authorities to introduce lengthy power cuts, hampering hundreds of industries across the island.
"This year, too, the northeast monsoon has ended with rainfall that is well below average," Deputy Chief of the Meteorology Department, Jayatilaka Banda, told Reuters.
"In many areas, rainfall has been below 50 percent of usual. There is a very serious dry condition," he said.
The Indian Ocean island has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectric plants, usually starts around the third week of May.
A senior official for the state power monopoly Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) said water storage at the country's six main hydropower reservoirs was at 25 percent of capacity as of Tuesday morning.
"We feel we can manage without power cuts, given the additions we have made to the grid. Unfortunately, that is not an absolute guarantee," said the official, who declined to be identified.
The CEB has said it planned to reduce dependence on hydropower to about 57 percent by mid-1997 by building more thermal power plants.

Sri Lanka's total power generating capacity of about 1,250 megawatts has been boosted by the addition of 70 MW from new small thermal power plants. Another 40 MW is to be added next month, the official said.
The government has asked the private sector industries to generate their own power and sell electricity to the CEB to augment its existing supply.
"It has encouraged many people to generate their own electricity and reduce the burden on the grid. But only a few of our industrialists can afford to do it," Amerasinghe said.
A new diesel plant by the CEB generating 155 MW is expected to be commissioned in June, the CEB official said.
But industries are also worried over the possibility of a price hike due increased diesel usage as against cheaper hydropower.
"The CEB is going to be burdened with a massive diesel bill. It has to be passed on to consumers," Amerasinghe said.
Last year, Sri Lanka's Ceylon Petroleum Corporation imported 600,000 tonnes of diesel, double that of its original estimate for the year, because of the drought.
